And the fact that dialectical, or dialectically sublated, existence is always a certain dialectical movement or becoming is expressed in the concepts of Vermittlung and vermitteln.
Vermittlung means “mediation,” while vermitteln means “to mediate,” “to act as an intermediary.”
In dialectical usage, however, Vermittlung stands in contrast to Unmittelbarkeit, or “immediacy.”
Unmittelbar sein means to “be” or “exist immediately.” By contrast, vermittelt sein means to “be” or “exist”—if one may put it this way—mediately.

Russian cannot express this naturally, because the obvious word has a completely different meaning. We are therefore once again forced to invent artificial and rather cumbersome technical terms such as “mediation,” “to mediate,” “mediatedly,” and so on.
But the words themselves are not important. What matters is what they express or conceptualize.
And after everything we have said, the meaning should now be clear.
Let us return to our example of discourse.
The “thetic” opinion, the thesis, is stated completely immediately and without reference to any other opinion.
The “antithetical” opinion, the antithesis, is stated in relation to a thesis because it is directed precisely against that thesis.
Yet the antithesis too is immediate insofar as it does not contain the thesis—precisely because it negates it.
The “synthetic” opinion, by contrast, is connected both with the thesis and with the antithesis, and it is mediated by the latter.
The antithesis serves, as we say, as an “intermediary” between the synthesis and the thesis.
The synthesis differs from the thesis only because, so to speak, it sees the thesis through the antithesis, or “by means of” it.
It is “synthetic” because it has been sublated—that is, because it appears as the result of an argument.
And the “process” of the argument is nothing other than the intervention of the antithesis. The antithesis, so to speak, “persuades” the thesis to “become” a synthesis.
If you like, the antithesis is nothing other than the thesis’s becoming synthesis.
“Mediation,” then, is nothing other than the appearance or intervention of the antithesis—its activity and realization.
But the antithesis itself is nothing other than realized “negativity.”
So we can say that the source, nerve, or driving force of dialectic is “mediation.”
Only mediated being, existence, or entity is dialectical, because only mediated being includes “negativity.”
In other words, the dialectical entity is “mediated” by a kind of self-negation that preserves and raises what it negates.
And this means that a “mediated,” dialectical entity never exists merely in a “simple” way or merely “for others.” It also exists “for itself.”
To negate oneself consciously, after all, one must in some sense know oneself, be aware of oneself, understand oneself.
One must, so to speak, “reflect” oneself back into oneself, becoming one’s own reflection or “self-reflection” (die Reflexion in sich selbst).
The dialectical entity therefore exists and acts not “immediately” but reflectively, precisely because it is itself an “intermediary” between itself and its own existence.
This also means that its existence is conscious: it includes consciousness and experience of itself.
And it is an intermediary to itself only because it negates itself dialectically.
In short, every “mediated,” dialectical entity always and everywhere includes self-consciousness. It is therefore a kind of conscious “I.”
Conversely, every “I” is necessarily dialectical or “mediated.”
Or again: every “mediated” form of existence is human, and every human form of existence is mediated.
So if mediation is nothing other than becoming, then becoming is nothing other than the becoming of the human being.
And the human being itself is nothing other than its own becoming.
Mediation, as the realization of dialectic, therefore humanizes being, existence, and the “thing,” transforming the latter into human being.
So if we want to speak concretely about realized—that is, real—dialectic, we must speak about humanity.

But before we come to this human realization of dialectic—before we speak about the human being as the being that realizes dialectic, and therefore before we turn to the concrete content of dialectic—we must say a little more about the formal character of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.
In other words, we must describe the general dialectical “framework” within which human existence unfolds.

We must define the “forms” of dialectical or “synthetic” existence—existence that is “total,” dialectically sublated, or “mediated”—while forgetting, as far as possible, that such existence is always and everywhere human.

In §§79–82 of the third edition of his Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences, Hegel gives just such a general and formal definition of dialectic and its three basic “constituent elements”: thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.
We can therefore use his three perfectly exact definitions.
Defining the thesis in §80, Hegel writes:

“Thought, as understanding [Verstand], stops—without going further—at the fixed determinacy [feste Bestimmtheit] of concepts and at the distinctness [Unterschiedenheit] they have in relation to other concepts. Such a limited and abstract entity or thing appears [gilt] to the understanding as subsisting [bestehend] and existing [seiend] for itself—that is, independently of everything else and, in particular, of the knowing subject.”
The “understanding” Hegel is speaking about here is simply ordinary, non-dialectical thought—the kind of thought we have associated with the “layperson” or the “scientist.”
As the passage makes clear, this kind of thought is governed exclusively by the category of “identity.”
For it, true concepts—and therefore the “things” corresponding to those concepts, as well as existence and being in general—are always identical with themselves.
They are “determined” once and for all, eternally and immutably. Hegel speaks of “fixed determinacy.”

Each thing is therefore determined by the unchanging relations between itself and other things—by its “distinctness in relation to others”—and ultimately by the “place” it occupies in the world or “cosmos.”

Yet the thing exists eternally as what it is, almost as though it were the only thing in the world. It does not essentially affect anything, nor is it essentially affected by anything else. And because nothing essential changes in it, it does not essentially change itself either.
This is what Hegel means when he says that it exists “for itself.”
The standpoint of the layperson or “scientist” would be entirely sufficient if existence were always and everywhere exactly what it appears to be from that standpoint.

That is, it would be sufficient if everything remained eternally identical with itself—or, in other words, if everything that exists were grounded in an eternal and immutable “essence” or “nature” given once and for all.
In short, this standpoint is sufficient for understanding non-dialectical, or natural, existence.
But Hegel is concerned with dialectical existence—which for us means human existence.
So the definition he gives in §80 is not complete.

It does not describe existence as a whole, but only one of its aspects: the thesis, in which “identity” predominates and which serves as the starting point of dialectical becoming—a becoming that coincides with the very “existence” or “being-there” of what exists.
This “thesis”—identity as a constituent element or aspect—is both real and necessary. Every dialectical being contains it.
Without it, we could not even speak.
We cannot designate an entity unless we can “determine” it—that is, “identify” or “recognize” it as “the same” thing and thereby distinguish it from all others.
But the thesis is not all there is.
Every dialectical being also contains the constituent element or aspect of “negativity,” which carries it from thesis into antithesis.

“The dialectical moment—that is, what is ‘rationally grasped through negation’ (see §79)—is the self-sublation [Sichaufheben] of these finite determinations [Bestimmungen] and their passage into their opposites.”
Unlike the understanding and its mode of thought, “reason” [Vernunft] and “rational thought” reveal the dialectical character of what exists by discovering “negativity” within it.
As we know, this negativity is the “nerve” of dialectic and can therefore be called, in Hegel’s narrower sense, the “dialectical moment.”
And this “negativity” is nothing other than the ability of an identical entity to cancel or sublate its own self-identity.
A dialectical—that is, negative, or more precisely negating—entity can itself negate the identical “essence” or “nature” given to it. This is what Hegel calls its “own self-sublation.”
By doing so, it becomes the opposite of what it was. Hegel calls this its “passage into its opposite.”

In other words, the entity can itself—while remaining the same entity, precisely this “identical” entity—break out of the fixed framework assigned to it by its supposedly unchanging relations with other things and with the world.
The entity can, so to speak, leave its “place” in the cosmos.
Hegel stresses that “negativity” cancels or sublates only finite determinations.
In other words, only a finite entity can be dialectical.
We will see later that this qualification is crucial.
For the moment, however, we do not need to dwell on it. Assuming that the dialectical entity is finite, we can say that it can dialectically sublate any one of its “determinations.”
Now, it is the dialectical entity itself that negates itself.
So even while negating itself, it remains the same entity.
But its unity is now “negative” or “negating”—that is, internally contradictory or dialectical.
And insofar as it is this kind of unity, it is no longer a “simple” unity or an “atom.” It is a unity of plurality: a “whole” or “totality.”
Ultimately, therefore, the dialectical entity is neither thesis nor antithesis but synthesis. “Totality” is what predominates within it.
Hegel defines the synthetic aspect of the dialectical entity in §82:

“The speculative, or positively rational, grasps [fasst … auf] the unity of determinations in their opposition. It is the affirmative [Affirmation] contained in their dissolution and their passage into the opposite.”

Then, in the first remark to the same paragraph, he explains why “negativity” does not lead to non-being—to the complete destruction of the being or entity that negates itself—but instead produces a new positive determination:

“Dialectic has a positive result because it has a determinate content; or, in other words, because its result is not in truth empty, abstract nothingness, but the negation of certain [gewissen] determinations. These determinations are contained in the result precisely because the result is not an immediate nothingness but a mediated result.”

If “negative-rational” or dialectical thought discovers the presence of “negativity”—that is, if it reveals the dialectical entity as antithesis—then the “positive-rational” aspect of dialectical thought discovers “totality” in that entity and thereby reveals it as synthesis.
This is possible because “negativity” is a concrete negation.
Dialectical negation is the negation of the thesis—that is, of something equal to itself, something identical and therefore also determinate.
The determinacy of what is negated therefore determines the negation itself.
The negation of A, precisely because it is the negation of A, possesses positive content.
And this preservation of what is negated, in and through the negation itself, gives the result of the negation a positive and determinate content.
This determinacy is “mediated” (vermittelt) by negation. More precisely, it is the result of negation.
And because of this mediation, the “negative” moment or aspect is just as present in the result as the “identical” moment or aspect.
The result is therefore genuinely a “totality.”
It is “A” insofar as A has been preserved within non-A—that is, insofar as A has been mediated through the “not.”
This sublated A—cancelled yet preserved and mediated—contributes the element of identity or determinacy to the totality.
But every finite determination can in turn be negated by a “negative” entity, and therefore also by a “total” entity, since totality includes the element of “negativity” within itself.
Every “synthesis” is therefore at the same time a new thesis: the starting point of another dialectical triad.
Taken as a whole, the first triad is only the first stage in the entity’s dialectical becoming—that is, in its dialectical existence.
